children.name: Polygenic Risk Scores
children.blurb: Polygenic risk scores summarize the combined effect of many common genetic variants on a trait or disease.

children.name: Gene Editing Guide Design
children.blurb: Gene editing guide design is the computational task of choosing short RNA sequences that direct a CRISPR nuclease to a specific genomic site while avoiding similar sequences elsewhere.

children.name: Pharmacogenomics
children.blurb: Pharmacogenomics studies how genetic variation affects drug response, including efficacy, dosing, and adverse reactions.

children.name: Epigenetic Aging Clocks
children.blurb: Epigenetic aging clocks are computational models that estimate a person's biological age from patterns of DNA methylation, often differing from chronological age.

children.name: Rare Disease Diagnosis
children.blurb: Rare disease diagnosis uses AI to search genomic sequences, clinical notes, and phenotype descriptions for patterns that match known rare conditions.

sections.body: Genomic medicine uses information from a person's DNA to guide diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment, and precision therapeutics narrows that guidance to the right drug or intervention for the right genetic profile. Artificial intelligence is now doing concrete work in this field, not just theoretical work. Machine learning models scan millions of genetic variants to estimate disease risk, prioritize likely causal variants in rare disease cases, and match unusual symptoms to known genetic conditions. In gene editing, AI helps design guide RNAs for CRISPR systems and predicts where an edit might land off target. In pharmacogenomics, models connect genetic variants to drug metabolism and response, and epigenetic clocks use DNA methylation patterns to estimate biological age. These tools mostly support researchers and clinicians, and they do not replace genetic counselors, laboratory confirmation, or clinical judgment.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work stands at different stages depending on the task, and variant calling from sequencing data is largely solved and highly automated, but interpreting what those variants mean remains hard. Polygenic risk scores can show statistical associations, yet they often perform less well when applied to populations that were not well represented in the training data. Gene editing design has improved at predicting on-target activity, but off-target effects, mosaicism, and delivery remain serious limits. Pharmacogenomic testing is clinically useful for a small number of gene drug pairs, while many proposed pairs still lack strong evidence. Epigenetic aging clocks are promising biomarkers, not diagnostic tools, and rare disease diagnosis still leaves many patients without a molecular answer. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, and the genomic pages here sit within that larger catalog, which shows both the breadth of the field and how much validation is still needed.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages below divide the field by the kind of genomic question being asked. A reader looking for risk prediction from many small genetic effects would start with Polygenic Risk Scores, which covers how models combine thousands of variants into a single estimate and where that estimate breaks down. Gene Editing Guide Design explains the computational side of choosing CRISPR guides and predicting off-target edits before any laboratory work begins. Pharmacogenomics focuses on gene drug interactions and the evidence needed to turn a variant into a prescribing decision. Epigenetic Aging Clocks describes how DNA methylation data is used to estimate biological age and what those estimates can and cannot say about health. Rare Disease Diagnosis brings together phenotype matching, variant prioritization, and the long diagnostic odyssey that AI aims to shorten. Together they show a field that is strong on pattern finding and still cautious about clinical proof.
